--- title: "Simple linear regression" author: "Prof. Maria Tackett" date: "08-27-2026" date-format: "MMMM DD, YYYY" footer: "[🔗 sta221-fa26.github.io](https://sta221-fa26.github.io)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true include-before: [ ''] html: output-file: 02-slr-notes.html html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- ## Announcements {.midi} - Complete [Lab 00](../labs/lab-00.html) if you have not done so - Accept GitHub invite (check your email or see the invite at ) - Need to be in course organization to access Lab 01 - Office hours start next week (see schedule on Canvas home page) - Lab 01 on Monday - Attendance is part of grade - Computing + hand written linear algebra exercises # Questions from last class? ## Topics - How regression is used to understand the relationship between multiple variables - Least squares estimation for the slope and intercept - Interpret the slope and intercept - Predict the response given a value of the predictor ## Computing set up ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(tidyverse) # for data wrangling library(tidymodels) # to format output library(knitr) # for formatting tables library(patchwork) # for arranging graphs # set default theme and larger font size for ggplot2 ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 14)) # set default figure parameters for knitr knitr::opts_chunk$set( fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.618, fig.retina = 3, dpi = 300, out.width = "80%" ) ``` ::: ## Data science workflow ![Source: Introduction to Regression Analysis: A Data Science Approach](images/02/data-science-workflow.png){fig-align="center"} ## Movie scores ::::: columns ::: {.column width="70%"} - Data behind the FiveThirtyEight (now defunct) story [*Be Suspicious Of Online Movie Ratings, Especially Fandango's*](https://web.archive.org/web/20230526120734/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/fandango-movies-ratings/?amp) - Data originally from the `fandango` data frame in **fivethirtyeight** package. Available in [`movie-scores.csv`](https://intro-regression.github.io/data/movie-scores.csv) - Contains every film released in 2014 and 2015 that has at least 30 fan reviews on Fandango, an IMDb score, Rotten Tomatoes critic and user ratings, and Metacritic critic and user scores ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ![](images/02/fandango.png){fig-alt="Fandango logo" width="200"} ![](images/02/imdb.png){fig-alt="IMDB logo" width="200"} ![](images/02/rotten-tomatoes.png){fig-alt="Rotten Tomatoes logo" width="200"} ![](images/02/metacritic.png){fig-alt="Metacritic logo" width="200"} ::: ::::: ## Data overview ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} movie_scores <- read_csv("https://intro-regression.github.io/data/movie-scores.csv") glimpse(movie_scores) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 146 Columns: 4 $ film "Avengers: Age of Ultron", "Cinderella", "Ant-Man", "Do… $ year 2015, 2015, 2015, 2015, 2015, 2015, 2015, 2014, 2015, 2… $ critics_score 74, 85, 80, 18, 14, 63, 42, 86, 99, 89, 84, 82, 99, 51,… $ audience_score 86, 80, 90, 84, 28, 62, 53, 64, 82, 87, 77, 60, 79, 70,… ``` ::: ::: ## Univariate exploratory data analysis (EDA) {.midi} The data set contains the "Tomatometer" score (**`critics_score`**) and audience score (**`audience_score`**) for 146 movies rated on rottentomatoes.com. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} p1 <- ggplot(data = movie_scores, mapping = aes(x = critics_score)) + geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", binwidth = 6) + labs(x = "Critics Score") p2 <- ggplot(data = movie_scores, mapping = aes(x = audience_score)) + geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", binwidth = 6) + labs(x = "Audience Score") p1 + p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Bivariate EDA ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(data = movie_scores, mapping = aes(x = critics_score, y = audience_score)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + labs(x = "Critics Score" , y = "Audience Score", title = "Audience vs. critics score", subtitle = "146 movies rated on rottentomatoes.com") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Bivariate EDA **Goal**: Fit a line to describe the relationship between the critics score and audience score. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Why fit a line? ::: {style="color: #799100"} **Prediction** ::: ::: question What is an example of a prediction question for the movie scores data set? ::: ## Your turn! Why fit a line? ::: {style="color : #799100"} **Inference** ::: ::: question What is an example of an inference question for the movie scores data set? ::: ![](images/august-27-qrcode.png){fig-align="center" width="45%"}
[app.wooclap.com/NNKYSFL](https://app.wooclap.com/NNKYSFL)
## Terminology ::::: columns ::: {.column width="30%"} - **Response,** $Y$: variable describing the outcome of interest - **Predictor,** $X$: variable we use to help understand the variability in the response ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Regression model A **regression model** is a function that describes the relationship between the response, $Y$, and the predictor, $X$. \begin{aligned} Y &= \color{black}{\textbf{Model}} + \text{Error} \\[8pt] &= \color{black}{f(X)} + \epsilon \\[8pt] & = \color{black}{E(Y|X)} + \epsilon \end{aligned} ## Regression model ::::: columns ::: {.column width="35%"} \begin{aligned} Y &= \color{purple}{\textbf{Model}} + \color{black}\textbf{Error} \\[8pt] &= \color{purple}{f(X)} + \color{black}\epsilon \\[8pt] &= \color{purple}{E(Y|X)} + \color{black}\epsilon \end{aligned} ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: $E(Y|X) = \mu_{Y|X}$, the mean value of $Y$ given a particular value of $X$. ## Regression model ::::: columns ::: {.column width="35%"} \begin{aligned} Y &= \color{purple}{\textbf{Model}} + \color{blue}{\textbf{Error}} \\[8pt] &= \color{purple}{f(X)} + \color{blue}{\epsilon}\\[8pt] &= \color{purple}{E(Y|X)} + \color{blue}{\epsilon}\\ \end{aligned} ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Determine $f(X)$ - **Goal**: Determine $f(X)$ - How do we determine $f(X)$ - Make an assumption about the functional form $f(X)$ (parametric model) - Use the data to fit a model based on that form # Simple linear regression (SLR) ## SLR: Statistical model (population) {.midi} When we have a quantitative response variable, $Y$, and a single quantitative predictor variable, $X$, we can use a (**simple) linear regression** model to describe the relationship between $Y$ and $X$. $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \epsilon$$ . . . - $\beta_1$: Population (true) slope of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ - $\beta_0$: Population (true) intercept of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ - $\epsilon$: Error terms with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2_{\epsilon}$ ## SLR: Regression equation (sample) $$\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X$$ - $\hat{\beta}_1$: Estimated (sample) slope of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ - $\hat{\beta}_0$: Estimated (sample) intercept of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ - No error term! . . . ::: question Why is there no error term in the estimated regression equation? ::: ## Estimating $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_0$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Residuals Given the data $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-slr_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: $$\text{residual} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted} = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$ ---


::: question How can we use the residuals to find the line that "best fits" the data? ::: ## Least squares line - The residual for the $i^{th}$ observation is $$\begin{aligned}e_i = \text{observed} - \text{predicted} &= y_i - \hat{y}_i \\ &= y_i - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1x_i)\end{aligned}$$ - The **sum of squared residuals** is $$e^2_1 + e^2_2 + \dots + e^2_n$$ - The **Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) line** is the one that minimizes the sum of squared residuals ## Least-squares estimator $\hat{\beta}_0$ ::: aside [Click here](https://intro-regression.github.io/appendix-linear.html#sec-least-sq-math) for full details on estimating $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$ . ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Slope and intercept ## Properties of least squares regression ::: incremental - The regression line goes through the center of mass point, the coordinates corresponding to mean $X$ and mean $Y$: $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}$ - The slope has the same sign as the correlation coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}$ - The sum of the residuals is approximately zero: $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i \approx 0$ - The residuals and values of the predictor variable are uncorrelated ::: ## Estimating the slope $$\large{\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}}$$
. . . $$\begin{aligned} s_X = 30.1688 \hspace{15mm} &s_Y = 20.0244 \hspace{15mm} r = 0.7814 \\[10pt]\hat{\beta}_1 &= 0.7814 \times \frac{20.0244}{30.1688} \\[8pt]&= \mathbf{0.5187}\end{aligned}$$ ## Estimating the intercept $$\large{\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}}$$
. . . $$\begin{aligned}\bar{x} = 60.8493 & \hspace{15mm} \bar{y} = 63.8767 \hspace{15mm} \hat{\beta}_1 = 0.5187 \\[10pt] \hat{\beta}_0 &= 63.8767 - 0.5187 \times 60.8493 \\[8pt] &= \mathbf{32.3142}\end{aligned}$$ ## Your turn! Interpret the slope ::: question The slope of the model for predicting audience score from critics score is 0.519 . Which of the following is the best interpretation of this value? ::: ![](images/august-27-qrcode.png){fig-align="center" width="45%"}
[app.wooclap.com/NNKYSFL](https://app.wooclap.com/NNKYSFL)
## Interpret the intercept ::: question 32.314 is the predicted mean audience score for what type of movies? ::: ## Is the intercept meaningful? ✅ **The intercept is meaningful in the context of the data if** - the predictor can feasibly take values equal to or near zero, or - there are values near zero in the observed data.
🛑 Otherwise, the intercept does not have a meaningful interpretation! # Prediction ## Prediction ::::: columns ::: {.column width="35%"} ![ Image from Rotten Tomatoes](images/02/odyssey.jpeg){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} The 2026 movie *The Odyssey* has critics score of 94% on [Rotten Tomatoes](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_odyssey_2026)\*. According to this model, what is the predicted audience score? $$\begin{aligned}\widehat{\text{audience}} &= 32.314 + 0.519 \times \text{critics} \\&= 32.314 + 0.519 \times 94 \\&= \mathbf{81.1}\end{aligned}$$ ::: ::::: . . . ::: question The actual audience score is 97%. What is the residual? What type of factors are included the residual? ::: \*score on 8/25/26 # Linear regression in R ## Fit the model Use the `lm()` function to fit a linear regression model
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} movie_fit <- lm(audience_score ~ critics_score, data = movie_scores) movie_fit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = audience_score ~ critics_score, data = movie_scores) Coefficients: (Intercept) critics_score 32.3155 0.5187 ``` ::: ::: ## Tidy results Use the `tidy()` function from the **broom** package (part of the **tidymodels** package) to "tidy" the model output
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|2"} movie_fit <- lm(audience_score ~ critics_score, data = movie_scores) tidy(movie_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 32.3 2.34 13.8 4.03e-28 2 critics_score 0.519 0.0345 15.0 2.70e-31 ``` ::: ::: ## Format results Use the `kable()` function from the **knitr** package to neatly format the results
::: {} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|2,3"} movie_fit <- lm(audience_score ~ critics_score, data = movie_scores) tidy(movie_fit) |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 32.316| 2.343| 13.795| 0| |critics_score | 0.519| 0.035| 15.028| 0| ::: ::: ::: ## Alternative: tidymodels syntax ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} movies_fit <- linear_reg() |> fit(audience_score ~ critics_score, data = movie_scores) tidy(movies_fit) |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 32.316| 2.343| 13.795| 0| |critics_score | 0.519| 0.035| 15.028| 0| ::: ::: ## Prediction Use the `predict()` function to compute predictions for new observations
**Single observation** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_movie <- tibble(critics_score = 94) predict(movie_fit, new_movie) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 81.07123 ``` ::: ::: ## Prediction Use the `predict()` function to compute predictions for new observations
**Multiple observations** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} more_new_movies <- tibble(critics_score = c(24, 70, 94)) predict(movie_fit, more_new_movies) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 44.76379 68.62297 81.07123 ``` ::: ::: ## Recap - Described how regression is used to understand the relationship between multiple variables - Used least squares to estimate the slope and intercept - Interpreted the slope and intercept for simple linear regression - Predicted the response given a value of the predictor ## Before next class - Complete [Lecture 03 prepare](../prepare/prepare-lec03.html) on model evaluation - Accept GitHub invite (check your email or see the invite at ) - Need to be in course organization to access Lab 01 - Office hours start next week (see schedule on Canvas home page) - Lab 01 on Monday - Attendance is part of grade - Computing + hand written linear algebra exercises

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
